title: God Structs Combining Unrelated Responsibilities
pattern: One large struct owns unrelated functional responsibilities or almost every application dependency (repositories, clients, config, utilities) and is passed around as an omniscient service/context instead of exposing cohesive components.
why_bad: Unrelated changes converge on one interface and dependency set, so a change to logging, config, or caching risks breaking unrelated user or socket logic, and the dependencies each operation actually requires become obscure. Taking `&mut self` on the whole struct unnecessarily restricts concurrent access to independent components, and the broad coupling increases maintenance and rebuild impact. It violates the Single Responsibility Principle and the Common Closure Principle.
detection: Look for structs holding independent database, network, logging, configuration, and business-entity handles from disparate architectural layers, coupled to methods that each use only a small disjoint subset of those fields. Source heuristics: more than 7-10 independent service handles, connections, or clients; roughly 10 or more fields or 20 or more public methods spanning different functional domains; or numerous cross-layer fields combined with dozens of public methods. Confirm responsibility fragmentation rather than classifying by size alone.
counterexample: The root application coordinator or composition root during startup, which exists purely to instantiate and link independent services before entering the execution loop; centralized application state in small CLI tools or tiny prototypes where simplicity outweighs separation of concerns; or a large but genuinely cohesive abstraction. Field count alone is not evidence of a God struct.
source: *Martin Fowler - Refactoring (1999)*, Chapter 3, "Large Class"; *Steve McConnell - Code Complete (2004)*, Chapter 6, "Working Classes" (Riel's heuristic of critical data members); *Robert C. Martin - Clean Architecture (2017)*, Chapter 7, "SRP"; John K. Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* (2018); *Robert C. Martin - Clean Code (2008)*, Chapter 10, "Classes" (Too Many Responsibilities).
